subject: maths
title: Inequalities

slides.heading: Inequalities — a range of solutions, not just one
slides.body: An inequality says one expression is greater than or less than another, so the solution is a whole range of values rather than a single number. You solve an inequality using the same inverse operations as an equation — with one critical exception: if you multiply or divide both sides by a negative number, the inequality sign must flip direction. The solution is shown on a number line, with open circles for strict inequalities (< or >) and closed circles for ≤ or ≥.
slides.note: Maximum 3 sentences. Plain English. No AQA references. What is this and why does it matter.

slides.heading: Inequality symbols and number line notation
slides.body: x > 3 means x is strictly greater than 3 (open circle at 3, arrow pointing right). x ≥ 3 means x is 3 or greater (closed circle at 3, arrow right). x < 3 means x is strictly less than 3 (open circle at 3, arrow left). A double inequality such as −2 < x ≤ 5 means x is between −2 and 5, not including −2 but including 5.
slides.note: Second concept slide — symbols table replaces formula slide.

slides.heading: Let's work through one
slides.question: Solve 4x − 1 ≥ 2x + 5 and represent the solution on a number line.

steps.instruction: Collect x terms on one side — subtract 2x from both sides.
Remove the −1 by adding 1 to both sides.
Divide both sides by 2. The sign stays the same (dividing by a positive).
Show on a number line: closed circle at x = 3 (because ≥ includes 3), arrow pointing right.

slides.heading: Watch out for this

mistakes.mistake: Solving correctly but writing the answer as an equation — e.g. getting x ≥ 3 but writing x = 3 as the final answer.
mistakes.correction: The solution to an inequality is always an inequality. Keep the inequality sign in your answer: x ≥ 3, not x = 3.

mistakes.mistake: Forgetting to flip the inequality sign when dividing by a negative number — e.g. solving −2x > 8 and writing x > −4 instead of x < −4.
mistakes.correction: Dividing (or multiplying) by a negative number reverses the inequality: −2x > 8 → x < −4. If you prefer, keep x positive throughout by rearranging first.

mistakes.mistake: Confusing open and closed circles on the number line — e.g. drawing a closed circle for x > 5 (which excludes 5) instead of an open circle.
mistakes.correction: Open circle: the value is NOT included (< or >). Closed circle: the value IS included (≤ or ≥).

slides.note: Minimum 2, maximum 3 mistakes. Specific not generic.

keyFacts.fact: Solve an inequality like an equation — but if you multiply or divide both sides by a negative, flip the inequality sign.
keyFacts.examTip: To avoid the flip, rearrange so the x coefficient stays positive. −3x < 12 → add 3x to both sides: 0 < 12 + 3x → 3x > −12 → x > −4.

keyFacts.fact: Open circle on a number line means the value is excluded (strict inequality < or >). Closed circle means the value is included (≤ or ≥).
keyFacts.examTip: Match the circle to the symbol: ≤ or ≥ → filled in; < or > → hollow.

keyFacts.fact: For a double inequality such as −3 < x ≤ 2, list the integers satisfying it — remembering to check each endpoint: −3 is excluded (strict <), 2 is included (≤).
keyFacts.examTip: Always check the endpoint values — one is usually excluded and the other included. Listing one too many or one too few is a very common error.

note: keyFacts: 2-4 entries. Exam-precise language. These are what Mabel writes into her notes.
